EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN – “THE LONG-RUN LEGACY OF THE COLONIAL MITA IN PERU”  

-----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Geographic sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (GRD).  

Why GRD?  
• Treatment is assigned strictly by an historically fixed, one-dimensional geographic boundary drawn by the colonial administration (the Mita frontier).  
• Households/districts located infinitesimally on either side of this boundary are plausibly identical in all pre-Mita characteristics except for exposure to the forced-labour institution.  
• Outcomes are observed only once (2001), so DID/event-study approaches that rely on pre-period outcomes are infeasible.  
• The GRD exploits local random-like assignment around the boundary, delivering causal estimates of persistent Mita effects, while allowing flexible non-parametric control for location.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (Tᵢ):  
Tᵢ = 1 if district centroid lies inside the historical Mita polygon, 0 otherwise.

Control group:  
Districts whose centroids fall just outside (e.g., ≤100 km) the Mita frontier; they share the same colonial governorate, altitude range, and ethnic composition but were legally exempt.

Running variable (Rᵢ):  
Signed shortest-path distance in kilometres from district centroid to the closest point on the Mita boundary.  
• Rᵢ < 0 → inside (treated)  
• Rᵢ > 0 → outside (control)

Cutoff: Rᵢ = 0.  

Treatment timing: Exposure began 1573 and ended 1812. In an RD we do not need the exact timing; we only require that assignment is determined by the cutoff and that it predates all modern outcomes.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
-----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the boundary in the absence of treatment.  
  Plausibility: Boundary was exogenously drawn by Spanish authorities for logistical reasons linked to Potosí distance, not local prosperity; altitude, soil quality, and pre-colonial population density change smoothly across most segments. Testable with covariate balance.  

A2. No precise sorting/manipulation of units relative to the boundary.  
  Plausibility: Modern district borders were set long after the Mita ended, so strategic positioning is impossible.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-boundary spillovers within chosen bandwidth).  
  Plausibility: Forced-labour obligations were non-transferable and specific to in-boundary villages; after abolition migration was limited by mountainous topography. We mitigate by using narrow bandwidths and robustness to excluding large towns.  

A4. Functional-form/bandwidth choice captures the correct local relationship.  
  Addressed via data-driven bandwidth selectors and local polynomial of order 1; check robustness to alternative bandwidths and higher-order polynomials.  

-----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
-----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Geographic confounders change discretely at the boundary (e.g., terrain, climate).  
  Mitigation: (i) show continuity of 15+ pre-treatment geographic variables; (ii) include flexible controls such as elevation range, slope, precipitation, and eco-zone dummies interacted with running variable.  

T2. Spatial spillovers (e.g., economic activity diffuses across the cutoff).  
  Mitigation: Estimate effects within increasingly narrower bandwidths (50 km, 25 km, 10 km). If spillovers bias estimates toward zero, effect size should rise as bandwidth narrows.  

T3. Post-Mita selective migration or differential district creation.  
  Mitigation: Verify that pre-1900 population density (1896 Peruvian census) is continuous. Re-estimate on 2001 outcomes using only indigenous-identified households to limit in-migration bias.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
-----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)   # fast data manipulation
library(sf)           # spatial operations
library(rdrobust)     # RD estimation
library(fixest)       # fixed-effects OLS for robustness
library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Load Data ----
dta <- fread("peru_mita_household.csv")         # household-level
border <- st_read("mita_boundary.shp")          # shapefile of historic boundary
districts <- st_read("peru_district_centroids.shp")

# ---- 2. Merge & Create Running Variable ----
# convert to same CRS
districts <- st_transform(districts, crs = st_crs(border))
border    <- st_transform(border,  st_crs(border))

# Shortest Euclidean distance; positive outside
dist_vec <- st_distance(districts, border)
districts$dist_km <- as.numeric(dist_vec)/1000
districts$inside  <- st_intersects(districts, border, sparse = FALSE)[,1]*1
districts$runvar  <- ifelse(districts$inside==1, -districts$dist_km, districts$dist_km)

# Merge with household data
dta <- merge(dta, st_drop_geometry(districts)[, c("DIST_ID","runvar","inside")],
             by = "DIST_ID", all.x = TRUE)

# ---- 3. Main Specification: Local Linear GRD ----
# Outcome: log equivalised household consumption
main_rd <- rdrobust(y = dta$ln_consumption, x = dta$runvar,
                    covs = dta[,.(elevation, slope, rainfall, pre1896_pop)],
                    p = 1,  h = NULL)        # data-driven Imbens-Kalyanaraman h

summary(main_rd)

# ---- 4. Robustness Check 1: Alternative Bandwidth 25 km ----
rd25 <- rdrobust(y = dta$ln_consumption, x = dta$runvar, h = 25)
summary(rd25)

# ---- 5. Robustness Check 2: Covariate Continuity ----
covariates <- c("elevation","slope","rainfall","pre1896_pop")
lapply(covariates, function(v){
  rdtest <- rdrobust(y = dta[[v]], x = dta$runvar, p = 1)
  return(list(var = v, coef = rdtest$coef[1], p = rdtest$pv[1]))
})

# ---- 6. Plot RD Graph ----
ggplot(dta[abs(runvar)<=100], aes(x=runvar, y=ln_consumption))+
  geom_point(alpha=.3)+
  geom_smooth(method="lm", formula = y ~ poly(x,1), se=FALSE, color="red")+
  labs(x="Distance to Mita boundary (km, + outside)", y="Log household consumption")
```

-----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition and prior historical evidence (e.g., coercive institutions hamper human capital and market integration) predict:  
• Mean household consumption inside the historic Mita: ~10–15 percent lower (i.e., RD point estimate ≈ −0.11 to −0.16 log points).  
• Child stunting rate: 3–5 pp higher.  
Magnitude likely attenuates with distance from Potosí within the treated side.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RD)  
-----------------------------------------------------------------
C1: No manipulation of running variable ................................... 1  
C2: Covariate continuity at cutoff ........................................ 0.8  
C3: Correct functional form / bandwidth choice ............................ 0.8  
C4: No spillovers / SUTVA within chosen window ............................ 0.7  
C5: Sufficient observations close to cutoff ............................... 1  

Total (out of 5) ........................................................ 4.3  

Overall, the geographic RD around the Mita frontier provides a transparent and powerful design to isolate the causal legacy of colonial forced labour on contemporary well-being in Peru.
